newsitem.title: UK: Tokyo oil spill throws spotlight on hull design.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo oil spill throws spotlight on hull design.

text.p: As Japan rushed 100 ships into Tokyo harbour to clean up a huge oil slick spewing out of a holed supertanker, fingers were already pointing at the vessel's single-hull design as a possible culprit.

Around 13,400 tonnes of crude oil spilled out of the Japanese-owned Diamond Grace on Tuesday before the massive tanker which was loaded with 257,000 tonnes of Middle East crude limped away from the reef where it ran aground.

Built with an old-style single-hull, Diamond Grace had been ordered just before the International Maritime Organisation ruled that all tankers commissioned after July 1993 should be built with a more protective double hull or mid-deck design.

Single-hulled tankers have only a few inches of steel to protect the cargo of oil, whereas double-hulled ships contain a space of several feet between the two steel layers, which acts as a safety buffer if the outer hull is ruptured.
Although shippers have complied with the IMO ruling on double-hulls, there are still those in the shipping world who voice doubts over the suitability of the design.
"Evidence does show that when you have a low energy grounding a double hull can sometimes avoid a spill," said Dr. Ian White, Managing Director of the International Tanker Owner Pollution Fund.
"But it depends how much damage is caused - if the damage is extensive it well may go through both hulls and that could lead to loss of buoyancy and make salvage more difficult."
Experts said it was too early to say whether a double-hull could have prevented Tuesday's oil spill - described as the worst of its kind by Japan's transport minister.
"It's pure speculation at this stage," said Drewry Shipping Consultants' Nigel Gardner.
White said once the full circumstances surrounding the accident were clear, experts would be in a better position to gauge the significance of the hull design.
He said immediate attention should focus on the clean up operation, which Japan appeared to be coping with well, following criticism of its handling of an earlier spill in January.
The hull design debate intensified last year when the single-hulled Sea Empress hit sharp rocks off the south west coast of Britain, causing around 65,000 tonnes of oil to gush out.
Shipping experts said an oil spill was prevented in the same area the previous year due to the double-bottom of a Norwegian oil tanker that ran aground there.
But it is unlikely a double-hull could have stopped the Exxon Valdez disaster in 1989, when a tanker smashed into the Alaskan seabed with enough force to break through two layers of steel.
Tests have shown double hulls are most efficient at preventing oil spills when ships run aground on sandy shores, often found around the United States.

But the design is widely believed to be less effective around Northern Europe where the seabed is littered with sharp rocks. Experts say the double layer can increase the risk of a ship breaking up if it scrapes on to rocks, as water can flood the inner cavity space, reducing buoyancy and forcing the vessel down.

Mark Jenkins, research director at shipbroker Simpson, Spence and Young said another danger of double-hulls was that in some cases there was a chance vapours could build up in the void space, increasing the danger of explosions.
"The double-hull is not the only prospective design capable of reducing oil spills in the event of tanker accidents," said Jenkins.

"Double-hulled tankers are somewhat unproven in terms of their long-term operating performance, as most have been built only recently...(this) warrants further research into the respective merits of other designs, so that the optimal environmentally friendly oil tanker can be devised."

But some shipping analysts say even if other designs have potential, they are unlikely to mature into the shipyard because of the United States' commitment to double-hulls. Tanker builders are wary of testing designs which would not win favour with the U.S.
